readerQuestion: Did this study show that my private AI chats are being exposed, and is there anything I should do?
readerPayoff: The reader understands that the finding concerns records of AI tasks people deliberately published — not ordinary private chats — and knows to share a checked result instead of an entire record.
headline: People published records of their AI work. Some contained passwords.
opening: A new study examined records people had published to let others inspect or replay an AI task. Those records held more than the answer on screen, and some included passwords and other private details. This does not mean ordinary private chats became public. The lesson is for anyone sharing AI work: send the checked result, not the whole work file.
newcomerBackground: Developers and researchers sometimes publish a record — a work file — so others can check how an AI task was done.
causalOutline: An AI tool can keep a visible answer plus the sealed part, which helps it continue earlier work.
A person publishes the complete work file so somebody else can check how the task was done, carrying both parts with it.
During the researchers' test period, a less-protected sibling model from the same provider could be made to accept the sealed part and reveal what it represented.
That route exposed private details in some public work files, including details that had not appeared in the visible conversation.
The researchers disclosed the route and report that the same attacks subsequently stopped working.
Sharing only the checked answer and approved evidence — not the whole work file — avoids that mismatch.

evidenceBoundary.establishes: The preprint reports real passwords, keys and personal details in the sampled public AI work files, including some details absent from the visible chat, and says the demonstrated attacks stopped working after disclosure.
evidenceBoundary.doesNotEstablish: It does not show that ordinary private consumer chats were published, that every AI work file contains private details or that the exact demonstrated attacks still work. The researchers lacked the original hidden text, so they cannot prove every recovered word was exact.

evidenceSequence: In an August 2026 preprint — a paper shared before independent academic review — Panfilov and colleagues took the sealed part from a published work file and handed it to a less-protected sibling model from the same provider. They called this an extraction attack.
Panfilov and colleagues examined 6,708 public AI work files from GitHub and Hugging Face; 328 of them — about 4.9% — contained at least one password, key or other private detail.

After removing duplicates and practice-test sessions with made-up characters, the study counted 704 distinct private details in real people's sessions. It does not say how many files those details came from.
The researchers made the sealed part readable with that attack, then compared the recovered text with the visible chat.
Most of those 704 private details also appeared in the visible chat; 64 appeared only in the sealed part.
The researchers lacked the original hidden text, so they cannot prove every recovered word was exact. That limit does not erase the credentials they report finding.

work.example: At work, a coding assistant diagnosing a broken website may see a deployment key — a code that can publish site changes. The work file from that session can carry the key even when the diagnosis on screen does not. The diagnosis is what your team wanted; the key was never invited to the meeting.

nonWork.example: At home, a travel assistant connected to your email may make a perfect Rome itinerary. Your friend needs the restaurant list, not the account details in the work file.

usefulLanding: Before sharing AI-assisted work, choose and check the answer you intend to send; do not publish the entire work file by default.
routingReason: This is a dated research finding with one immediate sharing lesson. The Daily can explain it concisely; a deeper treatment of technical safeguards belongs elsewhere only if readers need it.
